title: With the Samanas

teacherSummary.text: With the Samanas, Siddhartha learns fasting, enduring pain, and meditations that let his self pass into animals and objects. Yet after three years he concludes these are only escapes from the self, not true release. When rumors spread of Gotama, the Buddha, he and Govinda leave; Siddhartha masters the old Samana with his gaze before departing.

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: Excerpt-based (Middle School support track; this novel is above the grades 6–8 complexity band, so work from the passage your teacher selects). In “With the Samanas,” how does Hesse show self-denial as a path? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the passage, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the theme you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In With the Samanas, how does Hesse develop the idea of self-denial as a path? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the theme in the chapter helps build that idea. (You are reading the English translation by Gunther Olesch, Anke Dreher, Amy Coulter, Stefan Langer and Semyon Chaichenets, so word-choice evidence is the translators' English.)

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how With the Samanas develops the idea of self-denial as a path. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of theme and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim. (You are reading the English translation by Gunther Olesch, Anke Dreher, Amy Coulter, Stefan Langer and Semyon Chaichenets, so word-choice evidence is the translators' English.)

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of With the Samanas (where it begins, turns and ends) and its theme shape the reader's understanding of self-denial as a path. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what With the Samanas suggests about self-denial as a path. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's theme and characterization), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Hermann Hesse uses theme in With the Samanas to complicate the reader's understanding of self-denial as a path. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate With the Samanas within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of self-denial as a path responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read With the Samanas alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of self-denial as a path follows or bends those conventions, using the theme as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to With the Samanas and its treatment of self-denial as a path. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's theme and characterization, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads With the Samanas as evidence for a larger claim about self-denial as a path in Siddhartha. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads With the Samanas as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of self-denial as a path. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Siddhartha.

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: Siddhartha calls the Samanas' practices a 'brief numbing.' Do you agree? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are numbing, nirvana, festering, cowered, numbness. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check the definition. Here is the first: “It is fleeing from the self, it is a short escape of the agony of being a self, it is a short numbing of the senses against the pain and the pointlessness of life.” In this sentence it means: a dulling of feeling or pain. Word histories: “nirvana”: From Sanskrit nirvana "extinction," literally "a blowing out," from nir- "out" + va- "to blow." For the other words, look up the word history (Etymonline or the OED) and record the language of origin and the root meaning in your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Siddhartha would have known. Asceticism—strict self-denial—was a widespread spiritual practice in ancient India. Why does this chapter matter? Siddhartha discovers that discipline alone can become another form of illusion, a key turn in his quest. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for theme.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. The passage opens: “Silently, Siddhartha exposed himself to burning rays of the sun directly above, glowing with pain, glowing with thirst, and stood there, until he neither felt any pain nor thirst any more.” I stop and ask: what is the author doing here, and how does it connect to self-denial as a path? I circle “festering”, one of today's words, and ask why the author chose it over a plainer word. When I find theme, I underline it and write its effect in the margin, then I check my idea against the next sentence.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for theme.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of theme. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: Silently, Siddhartha exposed himself to burning rays of the sun directly above, glowing with pain, glowing with thirst, and stood there, until he neither felt any pain nor thirst any more. Silently, he stood there in the rainy season, from his hair the water was dripping over freezing shoulders, over freezing hips and legs, and the penitent stood there, until he could not feel the cold in his shoulders and legs any more, until they were silent, until they were quiet. Silently, he cowered in the thorny bushes, blood dripped from the burning skin, from festering wounds dripped pus, and Siddhartha stayed rigidly, stayed motionless, until no blood flowed any more, until nothing stung any more, until nothing burned any more.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their assigned rigor level.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Theme, Characterization, Imagery: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; the app shows the level your teacher assigned (for a 9–10 class, the HS Sophomore prompt reads: Analyze how With the Samanas develops the idea of self-denial as a path. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of theme and characterization shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim. (You are reading the English translation by Gunther Olesch, Anke Dreher, Amy Coulter, Stefan Langer and Semyon Chaichenets, so word-choice evidence is the translators' English.)) I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion from the 30 tiered questions (focus set for the class level): wait time, think-pair-share on DOK 3/4, follow-up probes.
segments.script: Let's talk. We move from what happens to why it matters to whether it's right. After each question I wait before calling on anyone: think first. Our anchor question: How does this chapter connect to the search for self-knowledge? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence, and end by writing one question of your own.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about self-denial as a path, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how theme shapes self-denial as a path. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.

provenance: Original Liber et Libri pilot content; modern contextual vocabulary definitions (curated, based on Princeton WordNet 3.0); word histories only where verified (Online Etymology Dictionary); quotations from the public-domain text.

routine: Bell-ringer: post one literal and one evaluative question; students jot before talking (wait time).
Discussion (10 min): run the focus questions for the class level in order, literal to evaluative; think-pair-share every DOK 3/4 item.
After each answer, use a follow-up probe before moving on; ask a second student to agree, extend or challenge.
Exit: each student writes one question of their own (student-generated) for tomorrow’s opener.
